cells.tense: Your strength moves outward now, and you are the one who decided where it goes.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are feeding right now, a person, a project, a habit, and say out loud which direction you want it to grow.
cells.core:
You are carrying strength for other people, and it is not costing you yourself. You can feel where the help stops because you have your own line, and you can feel where it keeps going because that is what you chose. What you pass to someone arrives with a shape, not a flood, and they can stand under it.

Where that gets bent is not in the act; it is in the choice of aim. The strength is right, but it can become a habit that feeds whatever is nearest rather than what you meant to grow. Before you pour, take the one second to see the direction. A single sentence about where the weight goes keeps the same generosity from turning into an accidental current.

cells.tense: Ahead of tomorrow, you are already at the door trying to hold everything that might come through it.
cells.ask: Before you say yes to the next request, wait five minutes and ask yourself one question: is this mine to carry?
cells.core:
You are trying to hold the future open with both arms. What has not arrived yet is already leaning on you, the favor nobody asked for, the crisis that has not happened, the person who might need something in a week. So you put your strength out there ahead of time, and the generosity turns into a fist that grips the air.

The grip is the problem. You can keep the same strength and hold it without forcing, which means letting the future arrive without your having to carry it early. The way back is not to give less but to check the moment before you give. What feels like moral clarity right now may be a habit of pre-empting every need. Asking yourself whether it is yours is what turns a vice grip into a hand.

cells.tense: For a while now you have stood at a closing door, strength in hand, not offering it.
cells.ask: Finish one thing today, however small, and notice that it is done, that it held, before you start the next.
cells.core:
Something got left behind. You have strength to share, and the offering stopped, so now the strength sits in you, unused, and the room around you feels a little emptier than it should. What you knew how to carry is still there; the arm is just not reaching.

What you can do now is not to feel your way back into others. It is to finish a thing and let it be finished, all the way through, without holding on. That completion is the release that makes room for strength to move again. It starts small and practical: you finish one thing, and the door you thought was closed shows itself as the same door you can leave.

cells.tense: You are already steadying something, and you tell it as though the situation handed you the role.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you have been calling part of the setup, and say out loud to yourself: this is something I chose to support.
cells.core:
You are already steadying someone or something. Your hands are in it, the help is real, but you give the credit to the situation, the need, or the role you were handed. The strength is moving out; your name is not on it. You tell the story as if it were a job that happened to you rather than the direction you picked.

That direction is yours. The next version is not a new action but a change in how you file it: once you name what you are actually growing, the support stops being maintenance and becomes a choice with a point. Nothing about the work needs to change today. What changes is that you stop being a contractor inside your own life.
cells.sheetLine: You are already the one tending it. Start saying so.
